The Proterozoic Eon. This vast period spans two point five billion to five hundred and forty-one million years ago, witnessing the rise of oxygen in the atmosphere, the evolution of multicellular life, and dramatic glaciation events. The name means "bearing early life" in Greek, and this eon is divided into three major eras: the Paleoproterozoic, Mesoproterozoic, and Neoproterozoic.

The Great Oxidation Event occurred around two point four billion years ago, flooding the atmosphere with oxygen and poisoning anaerobic microbes, forcing life to adapt. This stands as one of Earth's most profound ecological shifts. Snowball Earth episodes, especially during the Neoproterozoic, saw the entire planet freeze over multiple times, creating a white world covered in ice thousands of feet thick.

Multicellular organisms evolved near the end of the Proterozoic, including the Ediacara fauna—soft-bodied animals that predate the Cambrian by tens of millions of years. The Proterozoic supercontinent Rodinia broke apart during this eon, and later Pannotia assembled near its end. Eukaryotic cells, cells with a nucleus, arose during the Proterozoic through endosymbiosis, when one cell engulfed another.

By the end of the Proterozoic, the stage was set for the Cambrian Explosion—the rapid diversification of animal phyla. This eon follows the Archean, the era of simple microbial life that led to the Proterozoic, and connects directly to the Cambrian Period that followed.
